sources_considered.why: Primary security researchers describe testing a malicious skill against OpenClaw.
Versioned documentation describes host tool access and optional sandbox protections.
The project describes contemporaneous security work, qualifying claims of entirely absent protections.
Current documentation includes later developments and is not a reliable snapshot of January.

evidence_items.publisher: Cisco AI Threat and Security Research
evidence_items.locator: “A very particular set of skills,” now scanned by Cisco
evidence_items.explanation: Cisco describes invoking a third-party skill against OpenClaw, finding silent data exfiltration and instructions that bypassed the assistant's safety guidelines. This is direct evidence of the specified instruction-to-action weakness in the tested setup.

The documented default gives the main session host-level tool execution, explaining why malicious instructions can have consequences beyond generated text. The same section offers Docker sandboxes for non-main sessions, so exposure depends on configuration.

The announcement documents active security hardening while acknowledging that prompt injection remains unsolved. It qualifies an interpretation that OpenClaw had no protections, without disproving susceptibility.

unresolved_gaps: Cisco's article does not provide a complete execution transcript or enough configuration detail to estimate prevalence.
The Cisco page uses updated project naming; its January date is the page's displayed publication date, not an independently archived text timestamp.
The evidence does not establish every weakness that a literal reading of all might include.
